children.translated_text: "That is one alone, without a second"—
"<s>Brahman</s>"—thus says the <s>Upaniṣad</s>.
Does it not deny the existence
of anything other than <s>Brahman</s>?
Here we say: in the statement 'without a second,'
what compound is intended?
Is it a <s>tatpuruṣa</s> (determinative compound), or
is it a <s>bahuvrīhi</s> (possessive compound)? Let it be stated.
In the former case, the latter term
is primarily intended.
The referent of the word is that <s>Brahman</s>,
and what is other than it — either similar to it,
or opposed to it — in all three cases,
the other is not negated.
In the case of otherness or similarity,
a second is certainly established.
In the case of opposition, by the second,
a third or a first
is attained by <s>Brahman</s>, since it
is contradicted by the second.
Therefore, all the multitudes of meaning
beginning with the first, including the third,
having been touched by the second, thus
remain in their own state, unnegated.
Objection: The negative particle negates
everything other than <s>Brahman</s>.
Because the term 'second' is merely
an indication of everything.
Not so; no negation, for from this
a 'second' is not understood.
It denotes something other than that,
or opposed to it, or similar to it.
If the intended meaning is: '<s>Brahman</s> is that
which has no second,'
then the definitions stated as 'truth' and so forth
would become mis-characterizations.
If 'without a second' refers only to
the mere non-existence of the meaning of 'second,'
since the meaning of the negation is self-referential,
there would be no syntactic connection with the word '<s>Brahman</s>.'
The absence of a second would not there
be a qualifier of <s>Brahman</s>.
And if it were a qualifier, then that <s>Brahman</s>
would become a third or a first.
All the same consequences follow as before
when one analyzes it as a <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compound.
The first entities and those that are
third and so forth in the three worlds relative to <s>Brahman</s>—
because they are 'non-second' with respect to <s>Brahman</s>,
they remain in their own state, unnegated.
Moreover, in that <s>bahuvrīhi</s>
compound, when resorted to,
the meaning of the negation, which functions within the compound,
has no syntactic connection with an external referent.
If there were a connection with another meaning,
the genitive 'whose' (as in '<s>yasya</s>') would be appropriate.
The non-existence of a second entity
is not <s>Brahman</s> and not a qualifier.
Because of non-existence, what is non-existent cannot be <s>Brahman</s>,
nor can it be a qualifier.
Therefore, the real existence of the phenomenal world
is not negated by the <s>Advaita</s> (non-dual) scripture.
It is established by the strength of its own <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge)
and is also endorsed by scripture.
Therefore, '<s>Brahman</s> is without a second'—
the meaning of the scripture is stated thus:
There was not, is not, and will not be
one worthy of being counted as a second.
One who is equal to it or superior—
such a second is counted.
Since this entire universe is but a fraction
of a portion of its magnificence and power,
how could it attain the status
of being called a 'second'?
Just as the <s>Cola</s> king is the emperor,
without a second on the earth today—
this statement is aimed at precluding
any king equal to him,
but does not negate his servants, sons,
wives, and others.
Similarly, the multitudes of gods, demons, humans,
<s>Brahmā</s>, and billions of cosmic eggs—
these are untouched by <s>kleśa</s> (afflictions), <s>karma</s>, and
<s>vipāka</s> (karmic fruition) of the lord of all;
they are an ocean of the sixfold qualities beginning with <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge),
of inconceivable splendor—
drops and sprays from the ocean
of the majesty of <s>Viṣṇu</s>'s glory.
Who indeed, counting
the seven oceans on one's fingers,
could count the waves,
foam, bubbles, and sprays?
Just as there is only one sun
and no second in the sky—
by this statement, the rays
of the sun are not negated.
Just as that which is principal is not countable
in the counting of what is to be counted,
the count exists separately there,
because the countable is a different category.
"One quarter of him is all beings;
three quarters of him are the immortal in heaven."
Saying thus, he placed the entire universe
in this condition of being such.
"So great is his majesty,
yet he is greater than that."
"Where one knows nothing else,"
"He is the earth, the atmosphere, the interior,"
"He clearly creates fear of him"—
and so forth, these are the supreme <s>śrutis</s> (Vedic texts).
"For whom this entire <s>Brahmāṇḍa</s> (cosmic egg) and universe
is like an atom compared to <s>Meru</s>"—
these and similar texts establish
the 'such-ness' of all things in relation to it.
But the world of movable and immovable things
is a mere beginning of speech (a verbal construct);
born of modification, the immutable
root cause alone is real—
the effect is not different from the cause,
like sparks from fire;
with extensive illustrations from
clay, iron, seeds, and other examples—
fire cannot burn, nor can water
drown even a blade of grass,
nor can wind stir
without the empowerment of that power;
from the knowledge of one principal thing,
everything would become known—
by such Vedic statements
and the <s>āgamas</s> (sacred traditions) rooted in them,
this phenomenal world, consisting of consciousness and matter,
has <s>Brahman</s> as its self—this is its self-attainment;
thus it is established: the divine
<s>vibhūti</s> (glory) is not negated.
If it were negated, then because of the falsity
of the entire world and the <s>Vedas</s>,
all practical activities would be destroyed,
and so too would the cognition of <s>Brahman</s>.
"There is no contradiction even in falsity
because of the conventional reality
of perception and other <s>pramāṇas</s>"—this view
has already been refuted.
Therefore, the world, through the cognition of
the non-duality of <s>Brahman</s> arising from the <s>Upaniṣads</s>,
is not negated, because it is the <s>vibhūti</s> (glory)
of <s>Brahman</s>—this is established.
Objection: If the phenomenal world is real,
how can the cognition 'it does not exist' arise?
And if it is unreal, how can the cognition
'it exists' arise regarding it?
Likewise, the existence and non-existence of one thing
is impossible due to contradiction.
When the contradictory pair arising from
the cognitions of existence and non-existence converge—
because of the absence of certainty
regarding the meaning of either one—
the <s>Jainas</s> indeed assert the existence and non-existence
of the phenomenal world.
Having given precedence to the attainment of existence,
from the arising of the cognition 'it does not exist,'
the <s>Sāṅkhyas</s> have concluded
the eternal existence of the phenomenal world.
In the difficulty of the contradictory pair
arising from the cognitions of existence and non-existence,
for the purpose of resolving the contradiction,
by dividing into aspects of existence and non-existence,
some have said the phenomenal world is
indescribable as either existent or non-existent.
Others, thinking that existence and non-existence
are distributed according to distinctions of place, time, and so forth,
as in the case of a pot and such things,
have stated this arrangement.
Thus, when doubt has arisen
from the clash of disputants,
the determination there is made
according to the view of the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>.
If one cognized non-existence and existence
in the very nature of a pot,
then there would indeed be simultaneous existence
and non-existence in pots and such things.
Since the cognitions 'this exists here now'
and 'it does not exist' are of this nature—
the cognitions 'exists' and 'does not exist' do not arise
without distinction of place, time, and condition.
Therefore, the existence and non-existence of pots and such things
is determined by distinctions of place and so forth.
Since this is established, the possibility
of the [Advaitin's] argument does not exist here.
Objection: But the relation to place and so forth
is possible only for what exists.
The existence of the non-existent is not admitted
merely from its relation to place and time.
Relation requires two bases; therefore
existence of the existent would always obtain.
The existence of the non-existent through causal factors
as 'birth' is extremely implausible.
Therefore the phenomenal world, having beginning and end,
is placed within the category of the existent.
"What does not exist at the beginning and end
does not exist in the middle either, in the same way."
therefore, let it be accepted that what has established existence
is always existent.
The perpetual non-existence of the non-existent—
like a sky-flower—follows from its incapacity for production.
In non-existence there is no distinction
between what was previously non-existent and what is absolutely non-existent.
Taking <s>Śvetaketu</s> as the instance,

children.text: tat tvam ity api yac chrutam
children.translated_text: what has been heard as 'That thou art'—

children.text: tat tvam ity api yac chrutam

children.translated_text: in its sixth chapter,
how can the primary meaning be possible?
The conscious being denoted by the word 'thou'
is afflicted by wretchedness, sorrow, and pain;
the referent of 'that' is omniscient,
of true will, a boundless ocean of bliss—
how can there be identity of the two,
like light and darkness?
Whether the meaning of 'thou' is intrinsic or peripheral
(or the meaning of 'that' is distinctive),
the unity of meaning of the words 'that' and 'thou'
has been thoroughly precluded.
In such qualifiers as ignorance and omniscience,
suffering and bliss,
or in the qualifier or indication
of the root of consciousness—
due to the transference of contradictory qualities,
there would be difference between the meanings of 'thou' and 'that.'
By abandoning part of the denoted meaning,
the position that consciousness is one single manifestation—
'this is that bull' — that is the meaning
of the two words [tat tvam] — this is inelegant.
Because of distinctions of place, time, and condition,
even in a single substrate,
the transference of contradictory pairs is possible,
and thus 'this is that bull' is valid.
But for the self-luminous root of consciousness,
when contradictory pairs converge,
there is nothing to establish an arrangement
based on place, time, condition, and so forth.
In the self of consciousness, self-luminous,
from which all dualities have been shaken off—
because there is no delusion of the calamity of duality,
scripture would become purposeless.
By this, the having of true desires,
the being the cause of the world, and so forth,
are superimposed on the supreme through <s>māyā</s> (illusion) as a limiting adjunct,
while sorrow, delusion, and so forth
are on the <s>jīva</s> (individual soul) whose limiting adjunct is <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance)—
thus distributed—this is the view [of the Advaitins].
This view of the petty knowers of <s>Brahman</s>
has been refuted already.
Whether in the nature of pure consciousness or in the qualified—
the limiting adjuncts of <s>māyā</s>, <s>avidyā</s>, and so forth—
in the former case, there is complete confusion
due to the non-distinction of the supreme and the <s>jīva</s>;
in the latter case also, if consciousness,
even though qualified, is so,
the nature of consciousness is indeed undifferentiated;
by the limiting adjuncts of <s>māyā</s>, <s>avidyā</s>, and so forth,
it appears as if differentiated—this is delusion—
and also qualified (thus they think).
Do the peripheral properties not
touch the essential nature at all?
For surely, from cutting off the head of the stick-bearer,
<s>Devadatta</s> is not unharmed.
By the exclusion of the non-conscious aspect,
consciousness alone remains—
that this is the meaning of 'That thou art' and similar statements
is also unattractive.
In the absence of non-<s>Brahman</s> and non-self,
the inner consciousness remains.
The two words 'that' and 'thou' have as their domain
the identity of the <s>jīva</s> and the supreme.
That primary-sense identity
also rests on two real entities.
The alternative of difference and non-difference
that you have raised—
when bondage, which involves non-difference and difference, is unreal,
it is purposeless.
Non-difference, however, destroys difference
of the two entities that are its substrata;
difference is the mutual non-identity
of entities—thus of these two,
having accepted the nature of both,
of the alternatives of difference and non-difference,
the negation [of either is impossible]; therefore, by the negation of [your] speech,
you are refuted through contradiction.
The conceptualizing of connection, separateness, and non-separateness,
existence and non-existence—
is rejected by direct perceptual experience;
it is merely a parching of the throat (futile verbal exercise).
The cognition of blue in a blue thing—just as it is,
so too is the cognition of blue in a blue lotus.
"This is indeed a blue lotus"—
this shines forth directly to us.
Just as in the case of the known relation of conjunction,
though within the range of the senses,
there is a confusion of imposing false conceptualizations
of difference, non-difference, and other sophistries—
so too in the case of the relation of identity,
which is grounded in scripture and perception,
the delusion of false conceptual alternatives
is warded off by the staff of scripture.
Scripture, which is faultless and non-personal (<s>apauruṣeya</s>),
with the utmost reverence,
has repeatedly stated 'That thou art'—
the identity of <s>Brahman</s> and the <s>jīva</s>.
The liberated self, immersed in the pool of
<s>Brahmānanda</s> (the bliss of Brahman), flourishes in happiness.
But from the absence of a distinct enjoyer in the fruit,
<s>mokṣa</s> (liberation) would become purposeless.
For if only consciousness remains as a residue,
for whom would <s>mokṣa</s> be a fruit?
Moreover, what consciousness
transforms into the form of the phenomenal world?
Not the cognition of a pot, for even when it is absent
[the world] is seen.
For when it has not arisen
or when it has perished, that the entire world
does not exist—this cannot be said,
for if said, it would be contradicted by perception.
Nor is it another's consciousness, for even at its destruction
others are perceived.
Objection: Consciousness is undifferentiated and one;
there is no cognition of difference in it.
For pots and such things are differentiated,
but not consciousness, because it is self-luminous.
If the cognition of a pot does not shine
at the time of the cognition of a cloth—
not so, for indeed the pot does not shine [then],
but that [consciousness] does shine forth clearly.
If [you say] the consciousness associated with the pot
does not shine—
by the word 'associated with the pot' too,
is it that very consciousness or something else?
If it is that very one, it does shine; if it is another,
we do not speak of its shining.
Moreover, for this self-luminous [consciousness],
which is formless, there is not from itself
any error of apprehending diversity,
except through the diversity of objects.
Neither a substance nor a property of substance,
neither perceptible nor inferential—
the difference among knowable objects like pots
is merely of the nature of error.
If so, then the arising of the apprehension
of cognitive difference depends on that [error];
from what, and even more so, of that [error]—
the possibility of being ultimate reality.
Moreover, of that which is self-luminous,
whether by itself or by another,
the establishment of prior non-existence and the like would be —
by itself, to begin with, is not tenable,
because of the contradiction with its own existence,
and because non-existence has no fixed status.
Because for that whose luminosity is caused by itself,
even in the absence of itself, it is impossible.
Because it has no other object,
consciousness cannot [be established] by another either.
Moreover, difference and the like, which belong to the knowable,
cannot have the nature of a property of consciousness.
Like form and such, therefore <s>saṃvid</s> (consciousness)
is non-dual and self-luminous.
Therefore, relying on its differentiation,
whatever is expressed through conceptual thought and so forth,
that is merely a play of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) —
thus the knowers of <s>Brahman</s> know.
Indeed, this teaching of <s>Brahman</s>
shines among the faithful.
We are without faith,
we who seek reasoning.
Pertaining to each individual cognizer,
mutually distinct from one another,
they shine forth directly,
cognitions — like pleasure, pain, and so forth.
Of the difference indicated by the relata,
such as contact, desire, and the like,
it is indeed not the case that difference does not exist inherently,
nor is it accepted as non-perceptible.
If consciousness is accepted as
all-pervading, eternal, and one alone,
then everything should always appear,
or nothing ever at all.
For then, the proximity or remoteness
of the knowable object
cannot determine the functioning of cognition,
since it would pervade all like space.
Nor [is variation possible] through difference of causes,
since for what is eternal, those are absent.
Nor through multiplicity of essential nature,
since its oneness is accepted.
And then, a deaf and blind person and such
would apprehend sound and the like.
And the distinction of teacher and student and so forth
would be without cause.
But [you say]: apart from consciousness, for us
everything is verily nothing at all;
therefore 'everything should always appear'
— this objection is raised prematurely.
Tell me this, sir: what, does
blue and such not appear?
Does blue and such, while appearing,
not differ from consciousness?
In the first case, the agreeable functioning
of worldly and Vedic discourse is [destroyed],
since neither words, their meanings, and so forth,
nor anything else would appear.
In the second case, the desired non-duality
of consciousness would be contradicted.
If this manifold world of various forms
has consciousness as its essence,
and consciousness too has that as its essence,
then multiplicity follows.
Nor can one say that because it is a play of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance),
the determination of difference and non-difference is impossible.
For that [<s>avidyā</s>], when touched by the fire of reasoning,
becomes like an ornament of lac [that melts away].
For consider: if this <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance)
is held to be the mere absence of knowledge,
being of the nature of a non-entity,
it constrains nothing whatsoever.
If <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) is something other [than the absence of knowledge],
then the claim of non-determination of difference is well taken;
but the conceptualization that it is either a real thing
or something other than a real thing is not tenable for it.
That it is something other than knowledge —
this is a well-spoken statement.
If, further, its otherness too
is conceived by you as imagined through error,
then alas, in that case, <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) itself
would be knowledge in the ultimate sense.
Moreover, consciousness is pure and non-inert,
but this <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) is not like that.
By what reason then is it
not determined to be something entirely other?
Furthermore, this <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) of yours,
which has the form of the absence of that [knowledge] and so forth —
that knowledge — is it consciousness,
or the knowable, or the knower?
If [<s>avidyā</s> is the absence of] the knowable or the knower,
its removal by those two does not [follow].
For ignorance does not cease
from anything other than knowledge.
If [you say] it is consciousness itself — but then
its [<s>avidyā</s>'s] impossibility follows from the existence of that [consciousness].
Moreover, whether it [<s>avidyā</s>] is opposed to it [consciousness] —
nowhere is its [<s>avidyā</s>'s] existence possible,
since the entire world is pervaded
by knowledge alone, which is non-dual.
If the non-existence or the opposite
of consciousness is accepted,
then abandon far away
the thesis of the non-duality of consciousness.
Moreover, [you ask:] whose is this <s>avidyā</s>? Of which <s>jīva</s> (individual soul)?
And who is the <s>jīva</s> whose it is? — if [you respond] thus,
then surely this would be an irresolvable
mutual dependence.
Without the <s>jīva</s> there can be no <s>avidyā</s>,
and without <s>avidyā</s> there can be no <s>jīva</s>.
Nor is it comparable to seed and sprout,
since the origination of the <s>jīva</s> is untenable.
If [<s>avidyā</s> belongs] to <s>Brahman</s>, then how does it — being omniscient —
wander in delusion? — this is your [problem].
The dependence on the notion of the body as the self,
which is caused by <s>avidyā</s>, does not apply to you,
since the omniscience of <s>Brahman</s>
is heard [in scripture] to be its essential nature.
If [you say] omniscience is false
because it contains the appearance of difference,
then by the same token, why should [the teaching of non-duality]
not be false, like another word and so forth?
Just as the study of different words,
numbers, and so forth are the differentiators of the sciences,
and they contain the appearance of difference,
yet are valid — why should not [omniscience] be likewise?
If, even in the omniscient and eternally liberated one,
there is the possibility of ignorance,
then, as darkness in light,
it could never be removed by anything.
The statements about omniscience and such
have validity only at the empirical level;
but the ultimate validity belongs
to the statements of non-duality — [you say] thus.
We see no determining principle
other than your mere insistence.
If [<s>Brahman</s>] is the locus and <s>avidyā</s> is the counter-entity,
[and these are] mutually contradictory,
how is <s>Brahman</s>, which is of one flavor,
cognized as existent?
If <s>Brahman</s> is the locus in its subjective aspect,
and the counter-entity in its formal aspect,
whence is this difference of form?
If born from the grace of <s>avidyā</s>,
but that [<s>avidyā</s>] too depends on that [<s>Brahman</s>] —
there is again mutual dependence.
If [you say:] because <s>avidyā</s> is a non-entity,
(this is not a fault for it),
where have you seen a non-entity
serving as a defect for a real entity?
The fault of mutual dependence consists
in presupposing what is to be established.
It does not arise from being a real entity or a non-entity;
therefore this is not an answer.
Moreover, if <s>avidyā</s> is not a real entity,
whence then is this practical activity?
Nor is this activity accepted as being
like the activity regarding sky-flowers and the like.
Nor would your statement 'it is a non-entity'
establish its reality there.
If [you say] a real entity is negated
by the composite negative particle — that is not so.
A real entity that is first negated
by the composite negative particle,
is then restored by the distributive [negative],
and thus it has reality.
Therefore <s>avidyā</s>, which is neither an entity nor
a non-entity — when its power is present,
no difference whatsoever appeared —
never intend to say such a thing.
Moreover, this <s>avidyā</s>, which is resorted to as
the mother sustaining the world's functioning,
is it one alone,
or is it not one? Tell me this.
And the transmigrating soul who is its locus —
is he likewise one, or not one?
If it [<s>avidyā</s>] is one, then that one
was already removed by <s>Śuka</s>'s knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>
even earlier — so your effort
for liberation is pointless.
You may think: <s>Vāmadeva</s>, <s>Śuka</s>, and others
do not truly exist for you;
since <s>avidyā</s> was destroyed by their knowledge,
there is no <s>avidyā</s> now — this is the objection.
But the distinction of liberated and unliberated and so forth
is imagined by my own <s>avidyā</s>,
being perceived, like the variegated world
seen in my own dream.
Furthermore, [you say,] by <s>brahmavidyā</s> (knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>)
they attained liberation — thus;
that statement should be refuted by the reasoning
that dream-liberation is [equally valid].
But if by such reasoning
the world imagined by one's own <s>avidyā</s>
is established by another —
how would you respond?
The very reason you intend to establish
that your <s>avidyā</s> is the cause,
that same reason would apply to him as well,
just as in proving omniscience.
Thus, in your doctrine, which is vitiated
by mutually contradictory statements,
you are seen to be babbling incoherently,
as if saying 'I have a face.'
And just as the statement of dream-liberation
resembles the song of their liberation,
so it is for you too —
your effort for liberation is pointless.
Just as their liberation, which was non-existent,
is said to be existent through self-knowledge
previously, so likewise, [your liberation]
subsequently, through self-knowledge —
let it be called false even while non-existent,
yet declared to be future.
And there are scriptural statements
about things seen in dreams that serve as your illustrations.
But [you say]: this is not undesirable for me —
that liberation will not come about —
since the self is eternally liberated,
it is eternally established.
Then this would be like
invoking a ghost during a pacification ritual,
whereby the effort of acquiring
knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> is all the more pointless.
If, though eternally existent,
because it is obstructed by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance),
it is as if non-existent — then its manifestation
is accepted as the fruit of knowledge.
Just as gold and such, though in one's hand,
when forgotten, is searched for;
and just as that very thing, in one's hand,
when recognized, brings peace;
so too, due to non-comprehension of the
essential nature of the eternally liberated self,
[one remains] a transmigrator; and such non-existence
is revealed by <s>brahmavidyā</s> (knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>).
Alas, what is this manifestation
that is accepted as the fruit of knowledge?
Of the self-luminous essence of consciousness,
which abides in the state of its own nature —
is that consciousness itself? Or is it
'I am <s>Brahman</s>' — of what kind is it?
If it is self-awareness of one's own nature,
it is eternal — so it is not its [knowledge's] fruit.
If the consciousness 'I am <s>Brahman</s>'
is accepted as the manifestation,
but that, for you, is <s>brahmavidyā</s> itself —
how can it be the fruit of that same [knowledge]?
Moreover, in your view, it [that consciousness]
is produced from the sentence 'That thou art' and the like;
being originated, it is non-eternal —
so even for the liberated there would be fear.
Furthermore, those who know worldly practice [state that]
when the full cause is present,
if an effect does not arise,
they call that an obstruction.
Here, what is that which, having begun
to arise from its own cause,
does not attain origination
because it is obstructed by <s>avidyā</s>?
Not liberation, since it is eternally established;
nor the cognition 'I am <s>Brahman</s>' either.
For the cognition 'I am <s>Brahman</s>'
does not have a sufficient cause
in the transmigrating soul; so if it exists,
how is it obstructed?
Because it does not arise now
due to the absence of a cause;
not because it is obstructed —
therefore that talk [of obstruction] is misplaced.
Moreover, the claim that there is one <s>jīva</s> (individual soul) —
this does not accord with the nature of reality.
The <s>avidyā</s>, its association with it,
<s>jīva</s>-hood and so forth — all these are false for you.
The phenomenal oneness
is refuted by phenomenal [experience] itself,
since we perceive thousands
of transmigrating beings appearing simultaneously.
Until the complete cessation of <s>saṃsāra</s>,
the practical activities caused by that [plurality]
are perceived as unsubverted,
and are distinct from dream experiences.
Therefore, even the rational oneness [argument]
is refuted by reason [itself].
Mental dispositions that are mutually contradictory
are inferred from differences in behavior.
Other embodied beings, like one's own self,
cannot be denied.
Just as fire and such inferred [from smoke]
are distinct from the inference itself,
so too, the direct experience of others
— how is it not separate from other <s>jīvas</s>?
If it were not the case that another cognizer
is inferred through distinctive behavior,
all practical activity — both worldly and Vedic —
would be destroyed.
Nor [can one say that] through the limiting adjuncts,
the cognition of the division of the measurable and the measurer [arises],
since the same would apply to one's own body,
through the difference of head, hands, and so forth.
Just as there, when sensation arises
in the head, hands, feet, and so forth,
there is unifying recognition in spite of oneness,
the same would apply everywhere for you.
Due to the torments of death, the sufferings of hell,
and the distress of birth,
experiences of previous births, having long passed,
do not come within the scope of memory.
When pleasures and pains and such arise
simultaneously [in different beings],
there is confusion of substrata;
how then can there be the illusion of identity?
Nor does this worldly functioning operate
through individual <s>avidyā</s>s,
with multiple <s>jīvas</s> each having their own
individually projected visible world.
Those who are unaware of others' affairs,
each seeing only their own dream,
how could they carry on
that [worldly activity] which depends on association and such?
Moreover, self-luminosity,
all-pervasiveness, oneness, and eternality —
which you accept — would contradict
the non-duality of consciousness.
They are not consciousness itself; those properties,
even when consciousness is established,
are debated — as seen from the disputes about them,
and from the differentiation of their forms.
Nor are they established through error,
so as to be non-contradictory with non-duality.
For those qualities are established by
<s>Vedānta</s> statements that reveal the truth.
If bliss, self-luminosity,
eternality, greatness, and so forth
are held to be the very essence of <s>Brahman</s>,
even then, let this be examined:
Is what is designated as '<s>Brahman</s>'
merely that much? Or are bliss and the rest [also that]?
Or are they of that [<s>Brahman</s>], or, alternatively,
are they themselves what is called <s>Brahman</s>?
In the first case, the mention of each [attribute]
in both the Vedas and the world would be purposeless.
And by the previously stated method, difference [follows],
as well as being the cause of the world's origination and so forth.
For it is only after accepting <s>Brahman</s>
that the disputants debate about these [attributes].
In the second case, by those very [attributes]
<s>Brahman</s> would have a second.
In the third case, <s>Brahman</s> would be fragmented,
being merely that much at every step.
Or else <s>Brahman</s> would be a collection,
like a grove of trees and such.
Intensity and luminosity
are indeed distinct, though both reside in the sun.
Therefore, the meaning of no sentence whatsoever
is 'non-differentiation'—this is the demonstration.
If, through the removal of inertness, suffering, and the like,
they are held to function in one [entity] alone—
the words 'knowledge,' 'bliss,' and so on
do not [establish] that the existent has a second.
Are the exclusions non-existent altogether,
or existent, or neither?
If existent, the existent would have a second;
in the other case, they would have the nature of inertness and the like.
The statement of difference from both existent and non-existent
has already been refuted earlier.
And if that were the case, <s>Brahman</s>
would not be distinguished from a pot and the like.
Moreover, as for inertness and the like that are to be excluded—
when they do not convey contradictory meanings,
they cannot be excluded at all,
as with words having the same single meaning.
But when the counter-correlate is perceived,
the cognition of it as merely another entity—
that itself is absence—here too,
by the existent entities, your [<s>Brahman</s> having] a second [is established].
The differentiation of elements and elemental products
from both existent and non-existent—
from what is it ascertained? Is it
from perception and such, or from scripture?
The means of valid knowledge such as perception
determine their respective objects as they are—
they arise discriminating [their objects];
this much is self-witnessed.
Just as when blue is present before one,
the cognition does not speak of anything other than blueness;
the cognition of a white crystal
is not of the same form [as that of blue].
The cognition of sweetness in milk
is not the same as the cognition of bitterness in the <s>nimba</s> (neem) tree.
And all established practices,
both worldly and Vedic, are determinate.
True, the cognition exists; but if [you say]
its basis does not exist—that is not so.
If it [the cognition] exists, then let a basis
be postulated from it, since it is an effect.
If you say the sense-organs, inferential marks, and such have been postulated—
that is because of conformity with their existence.
Since simultaneity and sequence are incompatible
with discrimination and its establishment—
and since unity is impossible, difference is not
given in perception—whoever holds this delusion,
[suffers from] the failure to grasp the distinction between
difference, mutual absence, and discrimination.
The very own-nature of entities
that shines forth through perception
becomes the ground for the usage of 'difference'
in relation to the counter-correlate.
Just as the cognition of mere that-ness, being various,
is not the means for the usage of 'non-existence';
or just as the differences of shortness and longness
[co-exist] in a single six-<s>aṅgula</s> (finger-breadth) [entity];
thus, by the well-established
possession of multiple modes and forms,
the reality of the perceived phenomenal world
cannot be denied.
Scripture, being oriented toward action,
is not a valid means of knowledge in such a matter.
Even if it were valid, since its word-meanings are incapable
of logical connection, it does not convey [such meaning].
It is not non-existent, since cognition [attests it]; nor is the sublation

children.text: na sad ity api yan na tat
children.translated_text: that [shows] it is not real—that [argument] is unsound.

children.text: na sad ity api yan na tat

children.translated_text: Why is it not real simply by virtue of cognition?
From sublation it is not unreal—whence then [the unreality of] the world?
Therefore, this <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance)
is resorted to by you through <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) alone.
Moreover, the property characterized as falsity
of the phenomenal world of difference—
is it false or ultimately real?
The first option is not [tenable] straightforwardly.
If that [falsity] is itself false,
the reality of the phenomenal world is hard to deny.
Even if [falsity is] ultimately real,
by that very fact your non-duality is destroyed.
All the means of valid knowledge whatsoever
determine their respective objects as stated—
they shine forth to us, discriminating [objects]
from the non-existent and from other objects.
For example, the cognition that arises here
as 'there is a pot'—
it does not then allow the non-existence
of that [pot], or its being a cloth.
Now, as to what was said 'it exists'—is that
merely that much, or is 'pot' also [something more]?
Or is it something else? If merely that [existence],
then the non-duality of the existent follows.
If it is something else, then what is established is that
[the pot] is different from both the existent and non-existent.
If so, then 'Brahman exists'—
<s>Brahman</s> as held by the <s>Upaniṣads</s>—
would, like a pot, through being both existent and non-existent,
turn out to be indescribable for you as well.
By the very Vedic declarations of
bliss, truth, knowledge, and the like,
the non-such-ness of <s>Brahman</s> too
has been established by you yourself in this way.
And the statement of [the world's] being different
from both existent and non-existent is undermined.
Whatever is said of anything in any way,
that would apply to everything in the same way.
Therefore, the consciousness that arises
as 'it exists' with respect to pots and the like
reveals the ultimate reality of the
configuration of each respective object.
By means of the grounds for discrimination from
the homogeneous and the heterogeneous,
the existence of entities through their own respective
well-established forms—
that is reality; it is not an independent other.
How then can there be talk of non-duality there?
And the cognition of manifold forms
cannot be denied.
What was stated earlier, that the knowable
cannot be an attribute of cognition—
has anything been established by you
through that regarding consciousness, or not?
If so, there would be a contradiction with your thesis;
if not, your effort is in vain.
Therefore, cognitions whose differences
are naturally and clearly perceived—
do not attain unity with external
enduring [objects] such as pots.
From the invariable rule of co-apprehension,
no object other than consciousness would exist—
that which is self-luminous
and not dependent on another, that indeed [is consciousness].
The word 'self-luminosity'—
thus the learned declare.
For that, in whose non-appearance
a given object does not appear—
that [object] is not different from it,
like a false moon from the [real] moon.
And when cognition does not appear,
neither the self nor any object appears.
Thus, the phenomenal world clearly proceeds
as a transformation of consciousness.
Do not thus disparage [the phenomenal world]—
[it is protected] by the more powerful perception.
Those whose differences are protected [by perception]
do not conform to inference.
For 'I know this'—
clearly, by their mutual non-identity,
the triad shines forth directly;
this is self-witnessed by all.
And an inference that opposes
perception does not operate.
For the non-heat of fire
is not inferred from its being a substance.
Moreover, this reason is contradicted [by experience],
since the co-existence of the two [is observed].
For even according to you, consciousness
does not shine along with its own self.
The invariable rule of co-apprehension
is not [established] by each single cognition.
If this is not so, then everything together with universals
is the locus of cognition.
A continuous stream of pure consciousness alone,
free from the disturbance of blue and such—
as in deep sleep and similar [states], the object does not thus appear
as separate from cognition.
Therefore, cognition is real,
while the cognized object is unreal—so [you claim].
This is the prattle of one who has not examined
the self-contradiction in his own words.
For the invariable rule of co-apprehension
is thus undermined when this is the case.
Since that which appears even without [another]
shines also without that [other],
even without a pot, [consciousness] has shone;
likewise, the pot itself [shines] without a cloth.
